analysis.one_liner: Taxes oil companies' windfall profits and uses the money to cut transit fares and reward fuel-efficient cars.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees, then to a subcommittee, and died without a single vote before Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: During a 2001 gas price spike, this bill would have taxed oil and natural gas companies on profits above what a new federal board deemed 'reasonable' — at rates from 50% up to 100% of the excess. The money would have gone to tax credits of up to $6,000 for buyers of fuel-efficient cars assembled in the U.S. under union contracts, and to grants that cut bus and commuter rail fares. It was sent to three House committees, then a subcommittee, and never came back out.
analysis.who_benefits: Commuters and drivers would benefit twice: transit riders through fare reductions paid for by the oil tax, and buyers of fuel-efficient U.S.-made vehicles through tax credits of up to $6,000. Union-organized auto assembly plants would gain demand for the high-mileage vehicles the credit targets. Gasoline and heating-fuel customers benefit if the tax discourages the price spikes that prompted the bill.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an excise tax on oil and natural gas sellers equal to 50% of profits above a board-set 'reasonable profit' (rising to 100% above 105% of it), capturing revenue when companies profit from price spikes [S2] [S3].

Creates tax credits up to $6,000 for passenger vehicles with high fuel economy (35-65 mpg depending on type), limited to cars assembled in the U.S. by workers under collective bargaining agreements [S3].
Authorizes grants to bus and commuter rail operators to reduce fares for all passengers, funded directly by the windfall profits tax revenue [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and natural gas producers, refiners, and sellers pay the excise tax on any profit above the board's 'reasonable profit' determination. If companies pass some of the tax through, gasoline and heating fuel prices could rise at the margin, spreading a small cost to consumers. Taxpayers fund the new Reasonable Profits Board's operations.

drawbacks.text: A tax on profits above a government-set 'reasonable' level is hard to administer and could discourage domestic oil production and investment; the U.S. tried a windfall profits tax in 1980 and repealed it in 1988 amid complaints that it reduced domestic supply.

The vehicle credit is a nonrefundable tax credit, so its full value flows mainly to households that owe at least that much income tax, and it excludes any vehicle not assembled in the U.S. under a collective bargaining agreement [S3].

An appointed three-member Reasonable Profits Board would wield sweeping discretion to decide what profit is 'reasonable' for every sale of oil and gas, creating uncertainty for producers and potential pressure on prices [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits to commuters and car buyers are concrete and directly funded by the tax on oil profits, but the design is aggressive: a federal board setting 'reasonable profit' for every oil sale is administratively heavy, and history suggests such taxes can curb domestic production. The union-assembly and buy-American limits narrow who gets the car credit. On balance it is a straightforward transfer from oil windfall profits to transit riders and efficient-vehicle buyers, with real but arguable supply-side costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to three House committees and then a transportation subcommittee, and it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2003 without ever getting a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Dennis Kucinich introduced the bill on May 23, 2001, with 13 original cosponsors, during a period of rising gasoline prices [S3].
It was referred the same day to the Ways and Means, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Energy and Commerce committees [S1] [S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit, and no further action was recorded for the rest of the Congress [S5].
It gathered 18 cosponsors — 17 House Democrats and the one House Independent — but never reached a committee vote or the House floor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies are better off: no windfall profits tax was ever enacted, and their profits during the period remained untaxed by this provision. Commuters got no fare relief and no vehicle credits. The committees that held the bill were never required to take a public position on it.

for.name: Rep. Dennis Kucinich
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Gas Price Spike Act of 2001 and led it as principal sponsor.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, adding their names to support consideration.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: First-referred committee with jurisdiction over the tax provisions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and took no recorded action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee and House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no recorded action; the Highways and Transit Subcommittee held it from May 24, 2001 onward.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's one Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-controlled House never brought the bill to a vote.

industries.industry: Oil and natural gas producers and refiners
industries.note: The bill would tax 50-100% of their profits above a board-determined 'reasonable profit' whenever they sold crude oil, natural gas, or refined products [S3]. Industry interest in blocking it ran directly against consumers who would gain from fare subsidies and vehicle credits.
The fuel-efficient vehicle credit applies only to cars assembled in the U.S. under collective bargaining agreements, up to $6,000 per purchase, steering demand toward unionized domestic plants [S3].
Bus and commuter rail operators would receive federal grants to cut fares for all riders, paid from the windfall tax revenue [S3].
